items.name: agent-ask
items.title: Agent Ask
items.description: A structured question from an agent that needs input before it can continue — the UI surface for MCP elicitation. Takes a targeted `question`, a required `source` naming who is asking, a `fields` array describing what is needed (`text`, `number`, `confirm`, or `select` with concrete options and hints), an optional `explanation` giving the context that makes the question answerable, and three separate outcomes: `onRespond` with the collected values, `onDecline` to refuse this particular question and continue without the information, and `onCancel` to abandon the whole operation. Decline and cancel are deliberately distinct answers rather than one dismiss action, and both are rendered as visible first-class controls rather than hidden behind an overflow. `source` is required rather than optional because MCP's elicitation specification obliges a client to show which server is requesting input — 'some software wants your data' is not a question a user can safely answer without knowing the asker. The component prefers concrete options over free text: a select renders as labelled radio cards with optional hints, and a confirm renders as explicit Yes/No controls, because a question with buttons is answerable in a second where the same question in a text box is a small piece of homework. Submit stays disabled until every required field is answered. Holds perfectly still, since it is the user's turn under the system's turn-taking grammar — pair it with Agent Presence in the `asking` state. Purely presentational: it does not call a model and does not own the paused run. Use it for disambiguation between plausible matches and for missing parameters the agent cannot safely guess. Not for approving a consequential action the agent has already decided on (use AI Approval Gate), and not for a general chat input.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. MCP's elicitation spec requires that a client show which server is asking and offer both decline and cancel — `source` is therefore a required prop, and you should wire `onDecline` and `onCancel` rather than omitting them, even though the component tolerates their absence for non-MCP uses.

meta.engineeringNotes: Three decisions separate this from a chat prompt asking the same question. First, provenance is a required prop rather than an optional nicety: MCP obliges a client to show which server is requesting input, and it is also the only basis a user has for judging whether the question is safe to answer at all. Second, refusal is modelled as two distinct outcomes instead of one dismissal — declining answers 'not this information' while cancelling answers 'not this operation', and collapsing them would silently convert a narrow refusal into an abort. Third, the field types deliberately bias toward concrete options: `select` renders as labelled radio cards carrying optional hints (the disambiguation case, which is what elicitation is mostly used for, is far better served by 'Q3 Revenue Final.xlsx — edited 3 days ago' than by a text box), and `confirm` renders explicit Yes/No buttons rather than a checkbox, since a checkbox's unchecked state is ambiguous between 'no' and 'not answered'. That ambiguity matters here because submit is gated on required fields actually being answered. The component deliberately does not compose AI Action Toolbar for its actions despite the system's compose-don't-reinvent rule: the primary control is a real form submit button, and wrapping form submission inside a `role="toolbar"` would misreport the semantics to assistive technology for the sake of visual consistency. Text inputs are 16px on small viewports because anything smaller makes iOS Safari zoom the page on focus.
meta.motionNotes: Almost none, and that is the design. This is a user-turn surface under the turn-taking grammar (DESIGN.md §3a), which means it holds perfectly still — the absence of motion is precisely what signals that nothing proceeds until the user acts, and animating it would put it back in the same visual register as the machine's own busy states. The only motion present is the shared colour transition on hover, press and focus at `--pd-duration-instant`, matching every other control in the system, and it is dropped entirely under `prefers-reduced-motion` while the selected-state border and background still communicate which option is chosen. Entrance animation belongs to whatever surface reveals this component, not to the component itself — the same rule Confidence Meter and AI Action Toolbar hold.

items.name: agent-memory
items.title: Agent Memory
items.description: What an agent remembers about someone, where they can read it, correct it, or make it forget. Takes `memories`, each with `text`, an `origin` of 'stated' (the user said it) or 'inferred' (the agent picked it up) and an optional `source` ('Noticed across 6 conversations'). Handlers are `onEdit`, `onForget`, and optionally `onRestore`, `onForgetAll`, plus `paused` with `onPausedChange`. What the user said and what the agent guessed are listed separately, and inferred memories are framed as guesses worth checking, because a wrong inference quietly skews every later answer. Edits happen inline (Enter saves, Escape cancels). Forget fires immediately, while the row stays in place, struck through, with Undo, and focus moves to it. Pausing is described exactly: it stops new memories and doesn't erase old ones. Forget all needs a second confirming step that says it can't be undone. Use it in agent settings or a 'what do you know about me' panel. Not a chat history or a data export.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. `onForget` should really delete. The component keeps its own copy for Undo. When a user edits an inferred memory, store it as `stated`, because they have now said it.

meta.engineeringNotes: Built around the difference between stated and inferred memory. From the model side, an inferred preference that is wrong is worse than no memory, because it shapes answers without the user ever seeing why. So origin is a required field, the two kinds are listed in separate sections (the inferred list has a dashed border and reads 'Guesses from how you work'), and each memory can carry its source. Forgetting is honest about timing. `onForget` fires at once, so the caller can really delete it, and the component keeps a local snapshot with the original position so the row stays in place, struck through, with Undo. Focus moves to Undo after a forget and back to Forget after a restore, so keyboard users never lose their place. Pausing uses a real `role="switch"`, and its note says exactly what pausing does and doesn't do, because 'paused' is widely misread as 'deleted'. Forget all is the only irreversible action. It opens an inline confirmation with focus on Cancel and uses the destructive intent. A polite live region announces forgets and restores by content.
meta.motionNotes: Still, apart from direct feedback. It is the user's turn, so nothing moves unless the user acts. The pause switch thumb slides and its track colour changes at `--pd-duration-fast` on the standard curve. Hover colour changes run at `--pd-duration-instant`. Forgetting doesn't collapse or fade the row. It swaps to its struck-through state instantly and keeps its height, so the list doesn't shift under the pointer and Undo appears exactly where the user clicked. Everything is instant under prefers-reduced-motion.

items.name: agent-plan
items.title: Agent Plan
items.description: An agent's plan laid out for agreement before anything runs — the user can reorder steps, remove one, or add their own, then run the plan as edited. Takes `steps` (each with a `title`, optional `detail`, and an optional `needsApproval` flag for steps with external effects), an optional `title`, `onRun`, which receives the final ordered steps, an optional `onCancel`, and `allowAdd` to permit user-added steps. Steps that will stop for approval are labelled 'Asks for approval', and the header counts them, so the user knows before running where the agent will pause. Removing a step never deletes it outright: it stays in place struck through with an Undo, because a plan edit that cannot be seen or reversed is exactly the silent change the system exists to prevent. Reordering uses explicit move-up and move-down controls rather than drag, so it works identically by keyboard, touch and pointer, and every edit is announced through a live region. The run button reads 'Run edited plan' once anything changed. Plans are where an agent's misunderstanding becomes visible while it is still free to fix — once execution starts, a wrong step costs a tool call, a side effect, or a cancel and restart. This component is the agreement; execution belongs to Task Plan Runner. Composes AI Action Toolbar. Holds still, since it is the user's turn. Use it before multi-step runs, especially ones that touch external systems. Not for showing progress through a running plan.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Mark any step with an external effect as `needsApproval` so the user sees where the run will pause before it starts. This component does not execute steps — it hands the agreed plan to `onRun`.

meta.engineeringNotes: Separates agreeing on a plan from executing it, because the two need opposite designs: agreement is a still, editable surface where the user is in control, while execution is a moving status surface where the machine is. Merging them produces the common pattern where a plan is shown only as it starts running, which is too late to change it cheaply. Removal is modelled as a reversible state rather than a deletion — the step remains in place, struck through, numbered out of the sequence, with Undo — so an edit is always visible and never destructive. Reordering deliberately uses explicit up and down buttons instead of drag and drop: drag is pointer-first, hard to make accessible, and ambiguous on touch, while buttons behave identically across every input method and announce the resulting position through a live region (counting only steps that remain). The icon buttons are 32 pixels with hit areas extended vertically to 44, not horizontally, because the three controls sit side by side and overlapping hit areas would turn a near-miss into the wrong edit. Steps flagged `needsApproval` are labelled and counted in the header, so where the run will pause is known before it starts rather than discovered during it.
meta.motionNotes: Still, as a user-turn surface: nothing moves on its own and nothing shimmers. Removed steps drop to reduced opacity with a strikethrough rather than animating out, so an edit reads as a changed state instead of a disappearance and remains reversible in place. Reordering changes position immediately without a sliding animation — a swap that animates on every press would slow repeated keyboard moves and add motion to what is a precise, deliberate edit. The remaining motion is the shared colour transition on hover and focus at `--pd-duration-instant`, which drops to instant under prefers-reduced-motion.

items.name: agent-presence
items.title: Agent Presence
items.description: An agent's live state, expressed visually rather than described in text. Takes a `state` from an eleven-value vocabulary grounded in real protocol events — eight machine states (`queued`, `thinking`, `deciding`, `working`, `streaming`, `done`, `failed`, `cancelled`) and three hand-off states (`suggesting`, `asking`, `awaitingApproval`) — plus an optional `label` that overrides the state's default text, and an `onCancel` shown throughout the machine's turn. The organising rule is a turn-taking grammar: motion means the machine is busy, stillness means it is the user's turn. Machine states animate; hand-off states stop completely and sit brighter and heavier, so a user learns to read 'am I needed?' without reading a word. Three forms share the one vocabulary: `field` renders a cell matrix (the system's signature), `orb` renders a true Fibonacci-distributed sphere in CSS 3D for hero surfaces, and `line` renders three inline dots for status bars and table rows. The text label is the real signal and is announced through an `aria-live` region; the indicator itself is `aria-hidden` and supplementary. Purely presentational: it does not fetch, does not own the agent run, and does not interpret protocol events for you — map your stream's events to a state and pass it in. Use it anywhere an agent's activity needs to be visible in ordinary product UI. Not for showing the reasoning text itself (that is Reasoning Stream), not for a per-artifact generation progress bar (that is Generation Placeholder), and not for the post-result action strip (that is AI Action Toolbar).
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils` and the `pd-orb-spin` / `pd-cell-pulse` keyframes supplied by @pixeldosa/pixeldosa-theme's css block. The state vocabulary maps directly onto AG-UI events, OpenAI Responses lifecycle events, AI SDK stream parts, LangGraph interrupts and MCP elicitation — see the docs page for the mapping table.

meta.engineeringNotes: The load-bearing decision is that the eleven states split into two classes with opposite visual treatments rather than into eleven variations of one treatment. Every surveyed implementation renders 'thinking' and 'waiting for your approval' in the same register — something moving plus a line of text — but those are opposites: one means relax, the other means nothing proceeds until you act. Encoding that as motion-versus-stillness makes the most important question on the surface ('is it my turn?') answerable pre-attentively. The vocabulary itself is taken from protocol events rather than invented: `deciding` exists because AG-UI streams TOOL_CALL_ARGS before execution, so choosing an action is distinguishable from performing it; `queued` exists because OpenAI Responses emits it and accepted-but-not-started is not the same as working; `asking` maps to MCP elicitation and `awaitingApproval` to LangGraph's interrupt(). The orb uses a Fibonacci spiral distribution rather than the flat ring of dots most AI orbs use, which is what makes it read as a volume rather than a circle, and it is rendered with CSS 3D transforms inside a preserve-3d container so perspective supplies depth scaling for free — no per-frame JavaScript and no canvas. All three forms animate via CSS keyframes with per-element negative delays rather than a requestAnimationFrame loop; an earlier component in this system was rebuilt for exactly this reason, since re-rendering hundreds of React nodes per frame to nudge a transform is what makes these indicators stutter.
meta.motionNotes: Rotation speed is the state: 24s per revolution when queued, 12s thinking, 7s deciding, 4s working — so the same object communicates urgency through tempo rather than through a different animation per state, which is what lets states morph rather than cut. Terminal machine states (`done`, `failed`, `cancelled`) drop rotation entirely and settle to a smaller resting scale. Hand-off states stop dead: no keyframe is applied at all, and the dots transition to full scale and full opacity over `--pd-duration-slow`, so the arrival of the user's turn is a settling rather than a switch. Only `transform` and `opacity` animate, so every form composites on the GPU regardless of point count. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` every keyframe is disabled and each state still holds a visually distinct static configuration — differing scale and opacity per state — so the grammar survives with zero movement; the reduced-motion state is the same information without the motion, not a removal of the signal.

items.name: agent-steer
items.title: Agent Steer
items.description: Redirect a running agent without stopping it — 'not that file, this one'. Takes `running`, the `currentStep` the agent is on (so a redirect has something to be relative to), a caller-owned `steers` list where each redirect carries a real status — pending (sent, not yet acknowledged), queued (accepted, applies after the current step), applied, or declined with a reason — plus optional `suggestions` that fill the input for editing but never send, `onSteer(text, mode)`, and `onWithdraw(id)` for redirects the agent has not applied yet. Enter steers after the current step; interrupting mid-step is a separate, deliberate control, because stopping a tool call halfway can leave partial side effects. Status is never inferred from the key press: a redirect reads 'waiting for the agent' until the agent says otherwise, so it cannot look applied when it isn't. Use it beside a Live Status Line or Thinking Experience during long runs. Not a replacement for Stop, which stays visible, and not a chat composer.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. The steers list is yours: set each status from what the agent actually reports. Keep a Stop control visible next to it — steering is not a replacement for stopping.

meta.engineeringNotes: Built for the gap between Stop and wait: in real use, people change their minds mid-run, and today's agent UIs make them throw away the work so far to say so. Two decisions carry the trust. First, the component owns no status. Each redirect's status comes from the caller, meaning from the agent: it shows 'Sent — waiting for the agent' until the agent acknowledges, so pressing Enter never makes a redirect look like it has taken effect. Declined redirects show the agent's reason rather than disappearing. Second, the default applies at the next step boundary, where the agent can re-plan cleanly. Interrupting is a separate, secondary control, because abandoning a tool call mid-flight can leave half-written files or half-sent requests, and that risk should be chosen rather than triggered by the Enter key. Redirects that haven't been applied can be withdrawn. Suggestions fill the input rather than sending, so a one-tap redirect is still the user's sentence. The live region announces status changes to the latest redirect in words that match the visible text.
meta.motionNotes: Almost still. The agent's motion belongs to the status surface beside it, such as Live Status Line, not to the steer control. The one moving element is the shared `pd-shimmer` on a pending redirect's status. Under the turn-taking grammar that is the only state where work is genuinely happening on the machine's side for that redirect; queued, applied and declined are settled facts and hold still. Colour transitions on hover and focus run at `--pd-duration-instant`, and the shimmer falls back to static text under prefers-reduced-motion and where background-clip text is unsupported.

items.name: ai-action-toolbar
items.title: AI Action Toolbar
items.description: A keyboard-navigable toolbar of the standard post-generation actions on an AI-produced result — apply, explain, retry, regenerate, undo, report. Takes an `actions` array of `{ id, label, icon?, intent?, disabled?, busy? }` plus a single `onAction(actionId)` callback, and renders them as a row of real buttons with three levels of visual weight: `intent="primary"` is filled (the recommended action, e.g. Apply), `secondary` is bordered (reversible alternatives, e.g. Regenerate), and `quiet` is underline-only (meta actions that don't change the result, e.g. Explain, Report, Undo). An optional `message` renders leading status text before the actions, which is how confirmation rows like 'Changes applied. Undo' are expressed. Implements the ARIA toolbar pattern properly — the whole strip is one tab stop with arrow keys, Home and End moving within it and skipping disabled actions — rather than the natural-tab-order approximation most implementations use. Busy state is a per-action prop owned by the caller, not internal state, so it reflects the caller's real in-flight request; while any action is busy the others disable, since two concurrent actions on one result is never a coherent request. Purely presentational otherwise: it does not fetch, does not own an undo timer, and does not own the result it acts on. Use it attached to any AI output the user must now decide about. Not for a selection-triggered floating toolbar (use Selection Actions), a text diff needing per-hunk accept/reject (use Diff Accept), or a single whole-field proposal (use Smart Field) — this is the shared control strip those patterns compose, not a replacement for them.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils` and `class-variance-authority`. No icon set is bundled — pass your own `size-4` icons via each action's optional `icon` prop, matching how Smart Field and Selection Actions already take icons. Exactly one action should carry `intent="primary"`; the component does not enforce this, because a confirmation-only row (a lone quiet Undo) legitimately has none.

meta.engineeringNotes: An extraction, not new design: three already-shipped components had independently hand-rolled the same control strip. Smart Field renders Retry, Reject/Accept and an 'Value accepted. Undo' row; Diff Accept renders 'Changes applied. Undo' and a Regenerate-on-conflict button; Selection Actions renders Retry and Dismiss. Across those seven call sites exactly three button treatments recur verbatim — filled primary, bordered secondary, underline quiet — along with a character-for-character duplicated spinner SVG and a duplicated message+Undo confirmation row. Those three treatments became the CVA `intent` variants rather than being re-derived a fourth time. Two deliberate boundaries: (1) `busy` is a per-action prop rather than internal state, because every existing call site already holds the request and its AbortController, so owning a second copy here would let the toolbar's idea of 'in flight' drift from the caller's; (2) the undo *timer* stays with the consumer — Smart Field and Diff Accept both already run it inside their own status state machines, and absorbing it here would fight those machines rather than simplify them, so the toolbar renders the undo affordance while the consumer owns when it exists. The roving tabindex is kept as an action id rather than an index so the tab stop survives the actions array changing between renders, and it falls back to the first enabled action whenever the focused one becomes disabled — otherwise a toolbar whose focused action just disabled would have no tab stop at all and become unreachable by keyboard.
meta.motionNotes: Deliberately minimal, and the restraint is the decision. Colour-only transitions on hover and focus at `--pd-duration-instant` (100ms) with `--pd-ease-standard`, matching every other control in the system. There is no entrance animation, on purpose: this toolbar is always revealed by a container that already animates — Smart Field's proposal panel owns a grid-template-rows expand, Selection Actions owns a fade-and-scale — so a second entrance here would double-animate the same appearance. That mirrors Confidence Meter's rule that motion belongs to what wraps a primitive, not the primitive itself. The one continuous animation is the busy spinner, which is honest: it maps to a real in-flight request and stops when that request settles. Under prefers-reduced-motion the colour transitions drop to instant via `motion-reduce:transition-none`, while the spinner deliberately keeps rotating — removing it would leave a busy state with no visible indication at all, and the reduced-motion contract is a fallback that preserves legibility, not a removal.

items.name: ai-approval-gate
items.title: AI Approval Gate
items.description: A checkpoint before a consequential agent action — the human-in-the-loop surface for LangGraph's interrupt() and any equivalent pause. Takes an `action` phrased as a consequence the user can evaluate ('Send the Q3 summary to 243 contacts', never 'Execute send_email'), a `risk` level, a required `reversible` boolean, an optional `impact` list of countable facts describing the blast radius, optional `confidence` and `provenance`, optional `explanation` and `sources`, and three outcomes: `onApprove`, `onReject` and an optional `onEdit` for when the payload can genuinely be changed before it runs. `reversible` is required rather than optional because whether an action can be taken back is the single most decision-relevant fact on the surface and almost nothing surfaces it; it renders as a plain sentence rather than an icon. A `high` risk action renders its Approve control with the destructive treatment rather than the primary one, so a dangerous action never looks identical to a harmless confirmation. Composes this system's existing trust primitives rather than re-deriving them: Confidence Meter for certainty, AI Context Surface for the reasoning behind the proposal, and AI Action Toolbar for the decision strip — which means the decision controls inherit correct ARIA toolbar semantics, roving tabindex and busy handling for free. Holds perfectly still, since it is the user's turn under the turn-taking grammar; pair it with Agent Presence in the `awaitingApproval` state. Purely presentational: it does not execute the action or own the paused run. Use it before any external side effect — sending messages, spending money, publishing, deleting, or changing permissions. Not for disambiguating between options the agent cannot choose between (use Agent Ask), and not for reviewing a text rewrite hunk by hunk (use Diff Accept).
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Installing this pulls in AI Action Toolbar, AI Context Surface and Confidence Meter, which it composes. Phrase `action` as the consequence rather than the tool call — the whole component is worthless if the user cannot evaluate what they are approving.

meta.engineeringNotes: This is the payoff component for the system's trust thesis, and it is deliberately a composition rather than a new implementation: Confidence Meter, AI Context Surface and AI Action Toolbar are all consumed as-is, which is the 'compose existing trust primitives' rule (DESIGN.md §3.6) applied at the scale it was written for. Composing the toolbar rather than hand-rolling three buttons also means the decision strip inherits the real ARIA toolbar pattern — roving tabindex, arrow navigation, disabled-action skipping, busy handling — none of which a bespoke approval widget would have got right. Building it surfaced a genuine gap in that toolbar: it had no `destructive` intent, because nothing had needed one until an approval could be dangerous. Adding it there rather than special-casing here is the correct direction, since the house rule that a destructive action must never look identical to a harmless primary one applies system-wide. Two content decisions carry most of the value. `reversible` is a required prop rather than an optional flag: whether something can be undone determines how carefully the rest of the surface deserves to be read, and it renders as a plain sentence ('This cannot be undone') rather than an icon, because an icon is exactly the wrong weight for the most consequential fact present. The `impact` list exists because an approval without a scope is a yes/no question with the information removed — '243 recipients' is what makes the decision reviewable, and it uses tabular figures so the numbers align down the column.
meta.motionNotes: Deliberately still. This is a user-turn surface under the turn-taking grammar (DESIGN.md §3a): motion means the machine is busy, and animating an approval gate would put it in the same visual register as the agent's own working states — precisely backwards, since nothing here proceeds until the user acts. The only motion is inherited: the composed AI Action Toolbar's colour transitions on hover and focus at `--pd-duration-instant`, and its busy spinner while an approve or reject is in flight, which maps to a real request rather than decorating a wait. AI Context Surface brings its own grid-template-rows disclosure transition when expanded. Nothing animates on entrance — that belongs to whatever surface reveals this gate, the same rule Confidence Meter and AI Action Toolbar hold. Under prefers-reduced-motion every inherited transition drops to instant and the component loses nothing, because it never carried information in movement to begin with.

items.name: ai-context-surface
items.title: AI Context / Provenance Surface
items.description: A collapsed-by-default 'Why this?' disclosure showing an AI-produced value's explanation, sources, and model metadata — the folded-together answer to Citation Card, Source Viewer, and Thinking Indicator, none of which make sense without a chat thread. Takes optional explanation (plain-language reasoning text), sources (an array of { label, url?, snippet? }, rendered as a numbered list, each a link when a url is supplied), model (a string name), and generatedAt (a string or Date, formatted as a relative time within 24 hours or an absolute date otherwise). Renders nothing if none of these props are supplied. The trigger is a small, muted button; expanding it reveals a quiet bg-muted panel with the explanation first, sources second, and a model/timestamp footer line last. Use anywhere an AI-influenced value needs transparency available on demand without competing with the content it explains — a Smart Field proposal, a table cell, a classification result from Selection Actions. Not for a full chat/conversation transcript, and not for a single short provenance caption (Smart Field already has its own inline provenance prop for that).
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. `generatedAt` is formatted internally (relative within 24 hours via Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, an absolute locale date otherwise) rather than left to the consumer, since every consumer would otherwise reimplement the same relative-or-absolute decision. Renders `null` entirely when none of `explanation`/`sources`/`model`/`generatedAt` are supplied — a trigger with nothing behind it is worse than no component.

meta.engineeringNotes: Deliberately a disclosure (collapsed by default), not an always-visible panel: provenance detail is important to have available but wrong to force onto every view, since it would compete with the actual content for attention the moment it's always open — the same restraint Smart Field's inline `via {provenance}` caption already established, applied here at a larger, richer scale. Folds three previously-separate roadmap ideas (Citation Card, Source Viewer, Thinking Indicator) into one component because all three share the same real constraint this system cares about: working with zero chat thread present, unlike Vercel AI Elements' `Reasoning`/citation components, which are chat-message-scoped and excellent at that job specifically — competing with them there would be a bad trade, per the roadmap's own Reconciliation table. Timestamp formatting uses native `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` rather than a date-formatting dependency, keeping this primitive dependency-free like every other component in the registry.
meta.motionNotes: Expand/collapse reuses the same CSS grid-template-rows (0fr to 1fr) technique Smart Field's proposal panel and Diff Accept's conflict banner already use — a proven, token-free way to animate a height that depends on variable content, on --pd-duration-fast/--pd-ease-standard. The trigger's chevron rotates 90 degrees on open using --pd-duration-instant, matching Button's press-feedback timing, since it's an immediate state confirmation rather than content arriving. Under prefers-reduced-motion, both the panel's height transition and the chevron rotation drop via motion-reduce:transition-none, leaving the open/closed state instant but fully legible — aria-expanded already communicates the state to assistive technology regardless of the icon's rotation.

items.name: ai-form-fill
items.title: AI Form Fill
items.description: An agent filling out a form the user is already looking at — the embedded-in-product case rather than a chat. Takes a `fields` array describing each field and how to resolve its proposal, a controlled `values` record with `onValueChange`, an optional `onFill` hook that runs once per request so the whole batch can be fetched in a single round trip, and a required `triggerIcon` since no icon set is bundled. One action proposes values for every field at once, but every field is still reviewed on its own terms: each renders a Smart Field carrying its own confidence tier, provenance caption, explicit accept and reject, and one-step undo. The bulk request is the only thing that is bulk. There is deliberately no 'Accept all' control — per-field review is the entire point of the primitive underneath, and a button that let someone take twelve AI-proposed values in a single click would quietly undo the guarantee the whole AI tier is built on. Composes Smart Field, Field, AI Action Toolbar and Live Status Line, which transitively pulls Confidence Meter and Agent Presence. Fields propose together through a single token the block bumps, so no field gives up ownership of its own proposal state, undo window or in-flight request. Use it for enrichment and autofill inside real product forms — CRM records, onboarding, invoice details. Not for a single field, which is Smart Field used directly, and not for approving a consequential action, which is AI Approval Gate.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Installing this pulls in Smart Field, Field, AI Action Toolbar and Live Status Line, plus Confidence Meter and Agent Presence transitively. Fetch the whole batch once in `onFill` and have each field's `fetchProposal` read from that result — otherwise a five-field form makes five round trips for one user action.

meta.engineeringNotes: The load-bearing decision is what this block refuses to add. Bulk filling makes an 'Accept all' control feel obvious, and it is exactly wrong: Smart Field exists so that a proposed value is reviewed with its confidence and source before it becomes real data, and a single click that accepts twelve values with three different confidence tiers silently discards that. So the request is bulk and the review stays per-field — which is the honest reading of the system's 'nothing commits silently' rule rather than a convenience compromise. Making fields propose together required a small, consumer-driven addition to Smart Field rather than a workaround here: a `proposeToken` prop whose change requests a proposal. The alternatives were worse — remounting each field to re-fire `autoPropose` would have destroyed focus and in-flight requests, and hoisting proposal state into this block would have taken ownership of confidence, undo and abort away from the component that already does all of it correctly. The token deliberately ignores its first render, so mounting fields with a token present is not a request; that keeps unannounced fetching opt-in behind `autoPropose`, which is the posture the AI tier holds. `onFill` exists so the whole batch is one round trip: without it, a five-field form would make five separate model calls for a single user action, which is both slow and expensive in a way the user never asked for.
meta.motionNotes: Almost nothing belongs to this block. Every moving part is inherited: Smart Field's proposal panel expands via the house grid-template-rows transition, Live Status Line swaps its status text and carries Agent Presence's indicator, and AI Action Toolbar supplies the fill button's colour transitions and its busy spinner during the batch request. The block itself adds no entrance animation and no motion of its own, which is the correct outcome for a composition — one rhythm, set once in the motion tokens, applied by the parts rather than re-stated by the whole. The one motion decision made here is that the status line appears only while a fill is actually in flight, so the surface is completely still whenever the agent is not working and the user is reviewing. Under prefers-reduced-motion every inherited transition drops to instant and each composed component handles its own fallback.

items.name: ai-triage-table
items.title: AI Triage Table
items.description: Reviews many AI-proposed changes at once, organised around where human attention is needed rather than the order the AI produced them. Takes an `items` array of proposed changes — each with a `label`, an optional `before` value, the proposed `after` value, a `confidence` tier and an optional `provenance` — an optional `unchanged` list of things the AI examined and left alone, and an `onApply` callback that receives the ids the user accepted. Changes are grouped by confidence in attention order: low-confidence changes open first because they most need a human, medium follows, and high-confidence changes start collapsed to a count. Items the AI left unchanged collapse to a single line ('40 checked and left unchanged') so nobody scans forty rows to confirm nothing happened. Every row has its own Accept and Reject with a one-step Undo, before values are shown struck through beside the proposed value, and decisions are staged — nothing is written until Apply, which states how many changes it will commit and that unreviewed items stay as they are. It does not become an Accept-all: bulk acceptance exists only for the high-confidence group, and only after that group has been opened; low and medium changes must be decided individually. Composes AI Action Toolbar and Confidence Meter. Use it when AI output arrives in volume — enrichment across many records, bulk categorisation, data cleanup, batch corrections. Not for one field (use Smart Field), a single form (use AI Form Fill), or a text rewrite (use Diff Accept).
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Installing this pulls in AI Action Toolbar and Confidence Meter. Pass `unchanged` whenever you have it — showing what the AI deliberately left alone is half of what makes review cheap.

meta.engineeringNotes: Built in direct response to the audit burden: AI now produces changes faster than people can check them, and every earlier component in this system enables review without reducing it, which at volume turns the user into a full-time auditor. Triage reduces review in three ways. It orders by attention rather than by arrival — low confidence first, high confidence collapsed — so effort lands where errors are likely. It collapses what the AI left unchanged into a count, since confirming that nothing happened is otherwise the most tedious part of reviewing a batch. And it states consequences at the point of commitment ('Apply 5', 'not reviewed will stay as they are'). The hard boundary is that it must not become Accept-all by another name. Bulk acceptance is limited to the high-confidence group, and gated on that group having been opened — tracked as an explicit inspected set, with the reason stated in text rather than hidden behind a disabled button. Decisions are staged rather than committed, so every row's Undo is simply removing a staged decision, with no undo timer to manage. Collapsed groups use the house grid-template-rows pattern with overflow-hidden, and are marked inert while closed: a 0fr row hides content visually but otherwise leaves its buttons focusable and exposed to assistive technology.
meta.motionNotes: Deliberately quiet: this is a user-turn surface, so nothing moves on its own and nothing shimmers. Groups expand and collapse through the house grid-template-rows transition at `--pd-duration-fast`, the disclosure chevrons rotate at `--pd-duration-instant`, and a decided row fades to reduced opacity over `--pd-duration-fast` so the eye moves on to what remains without the row disappearing — its Undo stays reachable. Action colours transition through the composed AI Action Toolbar. There is no entrance animation and no motion tied to counts changing, since numbers updating in a review surface should read as information rather than event. Under prefers-reduced-motion every transition drops to instant and the grouping, counts and decided-state opacity still carry all the information.

items.name: autonomy-control
items.title: Autonomy Control
items.description: How much an agent may do without asking, as a setting people can actually read. Takes a `level`: 'ask' (propose everything), 'balanced' (handle small reversible things, ask before bigger ones) or 'act' (act, then report). It also takes the agent's real `actions`, each with a `risk` of low, medium or high, and optional `alwaysAsk` ids with `onAlwaysAskChange`. Instead of an abstract cautious-to-autonomous slider, each level is explained through those actions, and every row reads 'Asks first' or 'Does it, tells you', so choosing a level means choosing concrete outcomes. Risk sets a floor the user can raise but never lower: any action can be pinned to 'Always ask', and high-risk actions ask at every level. A live count ('Does 2 of 5 without asking') announces what a level change did. Use it in agent settings and onboarding. Not an approval prompt — that's AI Approval Gate, which this decides when to show.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. List real actions in the user's words, and put anything irreversible or external at `risk: "high"`. Enforce the same rule server-side: this control shows the policy, it doesn't enforce it.

meta.engineeringNotes: Research on agent products keeps finding people asking for lower automation and an off switch, while the 'match autonomy to risk' principle has no UI anywhere. Most autonomy settings fail because they are abstract. A slider labelled cautious-to-autonomous doesn't tell anyone what will happen to their inbox. So each level is explained through the agent's actual actions, with the outcome for each in words. The policy is a pure function of level and risk: 'ask' asks for everything, 'balanced' acts only on low risk, 'act' acts on low and medium. High risk asks at every level, and that is deliberately not configurable, because a setting that can turn off the approval for an irreversible send is a trap with a friendly label. User overrides only move in the safe direction: 'Always ask' pins an action to asking, and nothing un-pins the floor. Levels are native radios in a fieldset, so arrow keys, labels and form semantics come for free. The 'Does N of M without asking' count sits in a polite live region, because changing the level silently changes every row below it.
meta.motionNotes: Still. This is a settings surface and the user's turn, so nothing animates on its own. Selection and hover change background and border colour at `--pd-duration-instant`. Row outcomes swap text instantly when the level changes, not with a transition, so the new policy can be read the moment it applies. The focus ring follows the radio via `has-[:focus-visible]`. Under prefers-reduced-motion the colour transitions become instant.

items.name: button
items.title: Button
items.description: A clickable control that triggers an action. Renders a native button element, or any element via the asChild prop when the trigger must be a link. Supports six visual variants (default, secondary, outline, ghost, destructive, link), four sizes including a square icon size, and a loading state that blocks interaction while announcing itself as busy to assistive technology. Use for actions such as submitting, saving or opening a dialog; use a plain anchor for navigation that changes the URL.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`, which `npx shadcn init` creates. The press-feedback transition reads --pd-duration-instant and --pd-ease-standard; these are installed with this component, and the full token set arrives with the pixeldosa-theme item. When using asChild the rendered child receives aria-disabled rather than the disabled attribute, since non-button elements do not support it — handle click suppression in your own handler if the child is interactive.

meta.engineeringNotes: Variants are declared with CVA rather than conditional className strings so that the full variant matrix is a single serialisable object: it can be type-derived (VariantProps), documented from source, and extended by consumers via buttonVariants() without forking the component. The loading state disables the button but deliberately keeps it mounted and in the tab order — swapping a button for a spinner element moves focus to the document body mid-interaction, which is the most common accessibility regression in loading buttons. asChild uses Radix Slot instead of a render-prop so that ref forwarding and event composition are handled by the primitive rather than reimplemented here.
meta.motionNotes: The only motion is a 2% active-state scale, driven by CSS transition rather than Motion — a button appears dozens of times per page and forcing a JS animation runtime into it would be a bundle cost with no interaction benefit. Duration (instant, 100ms) and easing come from CSS custom properties generated from the motion tokens, so the press feedback stays in step with the rest of the system. The motion solves one problem: confirming that a press registered before the resulting state change lands. Under prefers-reduced-motion the transform is dropped entirely and the state remains legible through the background and focus-ring changes, which is a fallback rather than a silent removal.

items.name: card
items.title: Card
items.description: A bordered content container exposed as composable sub-components — Card, CardHeader, CardTitle, CardDescription, CardAction, CardContent, CardFooter, CardImage — rather than a single prop-driven component. Supports a vertical (default) and horizontal orientation via the orientation prop; CardImage reads the parent's orientation to switch between a top-rounded banner and a left-rounded side panel. Depth comes from a 1px border token rather than a shadow. Use to group related content on a page, including image-led listing cards and pricing cards built by composing these parts with your own content; use Dialog instead when the content needs to interrupt the user or block interaction.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`, which `npx shadcn init` creates. CardTitle and CardDescription render `div` elements, not heading tags, matching the wider shadcn/ui convention — supply your own heading element as content if the card needs to participate in the page's document outline. In `orientation="horizontal"`, Card does not auto-arrange its children into an image column and a content column — wrap the header/content/footer parts in your own flex column alongside CardImage.

meta.engineeringNotes: Exposed as eight composable parts rather than a single component with header/footer/title/image props, so a Block composing Card can rearrange or omit regions without fighting a monolithic API. A pricing card, for example, needs zero new Card capability — it composes entirely from the existing header/content/footer parts plus its own feature-list content, which is the intended test of whether something belongs in Card at all versus being a Block built on top of it. CVA now carries exactly one real variant axis, orientation, added because CardImage's rounding genuinely differs between a top banner (vertical) and a side panel (horizontal) — not spending it on density or interactive treatments yet, since no Block currently needs those. Depth uses border-border rather than a shadow, matching the system's dark-mode-first 'borders over shadows' decision documented in the design tokens.
meta.motionNotes: None. Card is compositional infrastructure with no interaction state of its own — motion belongs on components built on top of it (a future SpotlightCard or an interactive card treatment), not baked into the base primitive, per the pillar rule that motion must earn its place.

items.name: command-menu
items.title: Command Menu
items.description: A global, keyboard-first overlay (⌘K/Ctrl+K) for finding resources and running actions across an app. Renders as a centered floating panel on desktop and a full-width sheet under the sm breakpoint. Exports CommandMenu (the controlled root), CommandMenuInput, CommandMenuList (which auto-renders a live result-count announcer), CommandMenuEmpty, CommandMenuGroup, CommandMenuSeparator, and CommandMenuItem (accepts onSelect, an optional leading icon, and an optional keybind hint rendered as a kbd badge). Composes cmdk for the ARIA combobox/filter engine under a Radix Dialog for focus trapping, portalling and dismiss-on-escape/outside-click, with a token-driven CSS fade+scale for entrance/exit. Controlled-only: there is no internal open state, because the global shortcut listener has to live in the host app regardless. Use for apps with enough destinations or repeat actions that menu-hunting has real cost — dashboards, admin panels, developer tools; do not use it for a menu triggered from one visible button or row, use a Menu or ContextMenu instead.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. The host app owns the global ⌘K/Ctrl+K keydown listener and the `open` boolean — this component has no built-in trigger or shortcut binding, matching its controlled-only API. `CommandMenuItem`'s `keybind` prop is a single visible string (e.g. "⌘S"), not per-key badges; split it yourself if you need individually boxed keys.

meta.engineeringNotes: Uses cmdk for the input/list/filter engine rather than hand-rolling the ARIA combobox contract (input keeps DOM focus while aria-activedescendant points at the highlighted listbox option) — that contract is easy to get subtly wrong and cmdk is the same engine Vercel's own Geist command menu and shadcn/ui's command component build on. Radix Dialog wraps the whole thing rather than cmdk's own Command.Dialog variant, so PixelDosa keeps ownership of the visual contract instead of inheriting cmdk's default dialog chrome. Deliberately does NOT compose the shared `overlay` primitive (Motion-driven), despite that being the original plan: `overlay`'s AnimatePresence usage has a confirmed upstream bug (motiondivision/motion#3243) where the exiting panel and its full-viewport scrim sometimes never unmount, permanently blocking further page interaction after the first close — reproduced independently in Overlay's own existing demo, in both dev and production builds, so it is a primitive-level defect, not a composition mistake here. This component instead drives its fade+scale with a plain two-phase (mount in the closed state, flip to open on the next animation frame) CSS transition gated by a deterministic `setTimeout`-based delayed-unmount hook, reading the same `--pd-duration-fast`/`--pd-ease-standard` tokens `overlay` uses, so the visual result is identical while sidestepping the bug entirely. Recommend re-composing `overlay` here once its exit-completion issue is fixed upstream or worked around at the primitive level. Controlled-only open state (no internal fallback) because the consumer's global keydown listener already has to own the boolean. Also works around a second, unrelated composition gotcha: cmdk's own keydown handling on the Command root prevents Escape from reaching Radix's document-level dismissable-layer listener when cmdk is composed manually instead of via its own Command.Dialog, so Escape-to-close is handled explicitly rather than left to Radix alone. The result-count aria-live announcer is rendered automatically inside CommandMenuList via cmdk's useCommandState hook rather than left for every consumer to wire up. A separate kbd primitive was considered (per the component plan) and deliberately deferred: the keybind badge is a few lines of markup used only inside CommandMenuItem for v1, and extracting it into its own registry item before a second consumer needs it would be speculative.
meta.motionNotes: Fade (opacity) plus a slight scale-in (0.98 → 1) on both the scrim and panel, matching the shared overlay primitive's visual signature even though it isn't composed directly here (see engineeringNotes). Mounts in the closed state, then flips to the open data-state on the next animation frame so the browser actually has a 'from' value to transition from — setting both in the same commit would skip the transition entirely. Duration and easing come from --pd-duration-fast/--pd-ease-standard, the same tokens Overlay uses, so the timing stays in step with the rest of the system. Exit is handled by a matching deterministic delay (150ms, comfortably above the fast token) before the panel actually leaves the DOM, so the fade-out is never cut short. The mobile sheet layout (full-width, pinned near the viewport bottom under the sm breakpoint) intentionally keeps the same fade+scale rather than a directional slide-from-bottom, per the component plan's call to reuse one motion signature rather than add a second pattern for one breakpoint. Highlighted-row background change on CommandMenuItem uses --pd-duration-instant with --pd-ease-standard, matching Button's press-feedback timing, because it is state feedback rather than decoration. Under prefers-reduced-motion, both the panel/scrim transition and the row-highlight transition are removed via motion-reduce:transition-none (scale pinned to 100% via motion-reduce:scale-100), leaving the opacity and background-colour changes themselves intact so every state change stays legible without motion.

items.name: confidence-meter
items.title: Confidence Meter
items.description: A tiered (low/medium/high) confidence indicator with an optional provenance caption, shared by every AI-tier component that needs to communicate uncertainty about a proposed value, classification, or decision. Renders a three-bar filled/unfilled indicator (1/2/3 bars for low/medium/high) immediately followed by a text label ('Low confidence', 'Medium confidence', 'High confidence') — never a raw percentage, since that would claim precision the underlying model doesn't actually have. An optional provenance string renders as a second 'via {provenance}' caption alongside the tier. Purely presentational: no state, no async behaviour, a pure function of its props. Use anywhere an AI-proposed value or decision carries a confidence signal (Smart Field, Diff Accept, Selection Actions, and the future AI Approval Gate all compose this rather than each re-deriving their own indicator). Not for a full sources/context/explanation surface — use AI Context / Provenance Surface for that instead.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Has no client-side behaviour (no state, effects, or event handlers), so it carries no `"use client"` directive and can render on the server.

meta.engineeringNotes: Extracted from two already-shipped components (Smart Field, Selection Actions) that had independently hand-rolled the identical tiered indicator — the concrete signal per the system's own 'a component is not an island' rule that this belongs as its own primitive rather than being re-derived a third time. Confidence is a three-tier enum, not a raw number, by deliberate and unchanged decision from Smart Field's original plan: a fabricated percentage would claim precision the model doesn't actually have, and the system's token set has no 'success'/'warning' hue to spend on a red/yellow/green scale anyway — only `destructive` keeps real chroma. A numeric-score-to-tier bucketing input was considered and deferred: no current consumer has a raw calibrated score to map, and adding that path now would solve a hypothetical need rather than an observed one. Provenance is folded into this component as an optional prop rather than left as a sibling element every consumer composes separately, since the two already-shipped call sites both rendered them side by side anyway — one import now covers both.
meta.motionNotes: None, deliberately. This is a static presentational primitive with no state transitions of its own — any entrance/exit motion belongs to whatever container shows it (e.g. Smart Field's proposal panel), the same way Card's motion belongs to whatever wraps it, not to the primitive itself. Nothing here required a component-specific motion or reduced-motion branch, which is itself a signal the component is doing exactly what it needs to and no more.

items.name: diff-accept
items.title: Diff Accept
items.description: Reviews an AI-proposed text change as an inline word-level diff, resolved hunk by hunk rather than all-or-nothing. Takes baseValue (the text the proposal was generated against), value (the current live value), and proposedValue (the AI's suggested replacement), and computes the diff between baseValue and proposedValue using the diff (jsdiff) library. Each contiguous run of changed words becomes one hunk with its own Accept/Reject controls, shown inline as struck-through removed text and underlined/tinted added text. If value no longer matches baseValue — the underlying text changed since the proposal was generated — the diff is not shown; a conflict banner renders instead with an optional onRegenerate callback. Apply commits the current resolution (accepted hunks use the proposed text, pending or rejected hunks keep the original) via onApply, with a brief Undo affordance after. Use for reviewing AI rewrites of existing text — a bio, a description, any content field — where accepting some proposed changes and rejecting others is a real, expected outcome. Not for a single atomic value with no internal structure to partially accept — use smart-field for that.
items.docs: Uses diffWords from the diff package for word-level diffing — not a line-level diff, since this targets prose fields, not code. Unlike smart-field/ghost-input, this component does not call an AI provider itself; the consumer supplies an already-generated proposedValue (which may itself come from a smart-field-style fetch). baseValue must be exactly the text the proposal was generated against, not the current value, or the conflict guard will trigger on every render.

meta.engineeringNotes: Uses diff (jsdiff) for the actual word-level diff computation rather than hand-rolling a diff algorithm — the same relationship command-menu has with cmdk: a solved problem with real edge cases (Unicode, whitespace runs, word-boundary detection) not worth re-solving here. Hunks are grouped from the raw diff parts by merging consecutive added/removed runs into one reviewable unit, so a 'replace X with Y' shows as a single hunk with both the removal and the replacement, not two separate uncoordinated changes. Unresolved (pending) hunks default to the original text when merging, never the proposed one — an AI change only lands in the final result if a hunk is explicitly accepted, matching the system-wide 'never silently commit' rule. The status model is a three-state machine (reviewing/applied/done) rather than a single boolean: collapsing 'applied' and 'done' into one flag caused a real bug during development, where the conflict check (value !== baseValue, which becomes true immediately after Apply changes the live value) would incorrectly override the Undo affordance and show a conflict banner instead — the fix was ordering status checks so 'applied'/'done' short-circuit before the conflict check ever runs, since conflict is only a meaningful question while still reviewing.
meta.motionNotes: The system has no 'success'/'added' hue — destructive is the only token keeping real chroma — so additions and removals are distinguished primarily by text decoration (strikethrough for removed, underline plus a bg-accent/40 tint for added), not a red/green colour scheme, with destructive reserved for the removed text only since deletion is the one case that's legitimately danger-adjacent. This is also more accessible than colour alone, not just a token-budget workaround. Colour and background transitions on hunk resolution use --pd-duration-instant/--pd-ease-standard, matching Button's press-feedback timing, since resolving a hunk is an immediate state confirmation. Apply's brief settle state mirrors Smart Field's accept feedback for the same component family consistency. Under prefers-reduced-motion, all colour and background transitions drop via motion-reduce:transition-none, leaving the underlying decoration (strikethrough/underline) and resolved text fully legible without animation.

items.name: field
items.title: Field
items.description: A composable form-field wrapper providing Field, FieldLabel, FieldControl, FieldDescription and FieldError parts that share one generated id set and automatically wire aria-describedby and aria-invalid onto whatever control is placed inside FieldControl. Has no opinion on form-state management — works with plain useState, react-hook-form, or any other library. Use it as the base every labeled input, textarea or custom control composes on top of; it is the primitive that GhostInput, SmartField and every other AI-in-product component in this system builds on.
items.docs: FieldControl clones its single child rather than rendering a wrapper element, so pass exactly one React element (an <input>, <textarea>, or a component that forwards id/aria-invalid/aria-describedby/ref to a real form control) as its child.

meta.engineeringNotes: Built as a compound-component set sharing React context rather than a single Field component with many props, because form fields have a genuinely variable shape (some have descriptions, some don't; some controls are custom comboboxes, not <input>) and a large prop-driven API would force every consumer through the same limited combinations. FieldControl clones its child instead of rendering its own DOM node specifically so that input+icon or input+button compositions keep their existing layout — a wrapper div would break those. FieldDescription and FieldError register their presence into context via an effect so FieldControl's aria-describedby is always accurate even when a description or error mounts after the control, which happens constantly with async validation.
meta.motionNotes: No motion. This is a compound primitive other components render inside of, not a state that changes visibly on its own — anything Field itself animated would be inherited (and likely duplicated) by every component built on top of it. Error text appearing or disappearing is the one plausible candidate for a transition; it is left as a plain instantaneous swap here so that a consumer building a specific validation UX (e.g. GhostInput's inline error) chooses its own timing rather than inheriting one that might not fit.

items.name: generation-placeholder
items.title: Generation Placeholder
items.description: A layout-reserving placeholder for AI-generated media — image, video, or audio — that encodes real generation progress as a resolving dot field and then cross-fades into the finished artifact. Takes `status` (`queued` | `generating` | `processing` | `done` | `failed`), an optional `progress` between 0 and 1, a required `aspectRatio` that reserves the artifact's final bounds, and a `label` used as both the visible and announced status text. Renders its children only once `status` is `done`, so the component is a container rather than a sibling that gets swapped out — which is what prevents a layout shift at the moment the artifact appears. Two forms share one rendering engine: `field` draws a dot grid for image and video, `bars` draws a row of vertical bars for audio, where a rectangle of dots would misrepresent the medium. Progress is encoded spatially rather than temporally: every cell holds a stable pseudo-random threshold and resolves once progress passes it (ordered-dither logic), so the pattern itself carries the information and stays fully legible with all animation removed. `progress` is optional and never fabricated — omit it and the component shows an honest indeterminate wave rather than a synthetic percentage creeping toward 90%. Use it anywhere media is being generated. Not for streaming text (use Progressive Reveal, which appends whole items rather than refining in place), not for agent activity with no artifact attached, and not as a generic content skeleton — this component exists precisely because media generation progress is measurable, and a skeleton discards that.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils` and the `pd-fade-in` keyframe supplied by @pixeldosa/pixeldosa-theme's css block. `aspectRatio` is deliberately required rather than optional — it is the prop that prevents a layout shift when the artifact arrives, which is the whole reason this is a container component.

meta.engineeringNotes: The load-bearing decision is that progress is encoded spatially, not temporally. Each cell derives a stable pseudo-random threshold from its index (a deterministic sine hash, so the pattern never reshuffles between renders — a reshuffling field reads as noise rather than a resolve), and a cell resolves once `progress` passes its threshold. That is ordered-dither logic borrowed from halftone rendering: it produces an organic dissolve that is nonetheless an exact function of real progress, rather than a decorative animation that merely implies work. The payoff is the reduced-motion story, which is unusually strong for an animated component: because the information lives in the pattern rather than the movement, `prefers-reduced-motion` removes every transition and the progress stays completely legible — no fallback had to be invented. `progress` is optional with no synthetic fallback, deliberately: media generation genuinely reports steps (diffusion iterations, encoded frames) where text streaming does not, so a percentage here is measured rather than invented — the system's rule is not 'never show a number' but 'never invent precision you don't have', which is the same rule that makes Confidence Meter refuse one. `aspectRatio` is required because a media placeholder that resizes on completion causes a layout shift at exactly the moment the user's attention is on it. `processing` exists as a state separate from `generating` so a user is never told 'done' while an upscale or encode is still running. The requestAnimationFrame loop that drives indeterminate mode is not started at all when the component is determinate or motion is reduced, since an animation frame loop nobody can see is pure battery cost.
meta.motionNotes: Cells transition `transform: scale` at `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-standard`; because each cell's threshold differs, the resolve reads as a wave without any explicit stagger orchestration — the stagger is a free consequence of the threshold distribution. Indeterminate mode travels a phase offset across the same thresholds on a 2s loop, the single continuous animation in the component, and it maps to real ongoing work rather than decorating a wait. Completion is a cross-fade, never a pop: the artifact fades in over `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-decelerate` while the field is unmounted, so the two states morph rather than cut. Only `transform` and `opacity` animate, so the whole field composites on the GPU regardless of density. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` every transition is dropped and the wave loop never starts; cells snap to their correct scale and hold a static pattern, which costs nothing because progress was already spatial — the reduced-motion state is the same information without the movement, which is the fallback contract rather than a removal.

items.name: ghost-input
items.title: Ghost Input
items.description: A single-line text input with inline AI ghost-text completion: after the user pauses typing, a dimmed continuation appears past the caret, accepted with Tab or the right-arrow key (only when the caret is already at the end of the text) and dismissed with Escape. Takes a fetchSuggestion(value, signal) prop that the consumer implements against their own model — the component owns debouncing, request cancellation on every keystroke, staleness checking (a suggestion that doesn't continue the current text is discarded), and the accessible announcement of the suggestion via a live region. It never inserts text automatically; acceptance is always an explicit keypress. Use for reply drafting, search boxes, or any single-line field where predictive continuation should stay out of the way until the user asks for it. Not for multi-field or full-document autocomplete — this is a single <input>, not an editor.
items.docs: value/onValueChange are required — this is a controlled component only. fetchSuggestion must resolve to the FULL continued string (current value + completion), not just the completion tail; the component slices the tail itself and drops any result that doesn't start with the value it was requested for, so a response arriving after the user has kept typing can't overwrite what they see. Drops into <FieldControl> directly since id/aria-invalid/aria-describedby/ref all forward to the underlying <input>.

meta.engineeringNotes: The ghost text is rendered as a separate mirror div positioned exactly behind the real <input>, with the typed-text portion set to transparent — not as a styled fake caret or a contentEditable trick. This is the only approach that keeps native input behaviour (IME composition, selection, undo, autofill, screen-reader field semantics) completely intact, at the cost of the mirror div needing identical padding/font/line-height to the input, which is why both come from the same className. The whole request lifecycle — debounce timer, AbortController — lives in refs rather than state so that a rapid keystroke can synchronously cancel the previous request without waiting for a re-render; a state-based cancellation would let a slow response race a fast one and briefly show a stale suggestion. The right-arrow accept only fires when the caret is already at the end of the value (checked via selectionStart/selectionEnd), because otherwise it would silently hijack normal in-text cursor movement, which is a worse failure mode than requiring Tab.
meta.motionNotes: The suggestion's appearance is a plain opacity transition using duration.fast and easing.standard from the token scale — deliberately not a slide or typewriter reveal, both of which would misrepresent what happened: the whole continuation exists immediately (it was already fetched), so animating it in character-by-character would be a fabricated sense of the model 'typing', not a real progressive state. Under prefers-reduced-motion this reduces to a duration.instant swap via the same token path every other component in the system uses; nothing here required a component-specific reduced-motion branch, which is itself a signal the animation is doing the minimum necessary rather than something decorative.

items.name: inline-citations
items.title: Inline Citations
items.description: Claim-level sources that take one step to check. `CitedText` takes the answer's `sources` (id, title, url, publisher, date), numbers them in order and renders a numbered reference list underneath. `Cite` wraps one claim, takes `source` (an id or ids), the `quote` that supports it (or one quote per source) and `support`: 'quoted' or 'paraphrased'. Each claim gets a small numbered marker. On hover, keyboard focus or tap, a popover shows the supporting passage itself next to the claim, says whether the source quotes it or the agent summarised it, and links to 'Open at this passage', which deep-links with a URL text fragment so the source opens scrolled to the highlighted words. The claim is highlighted while its source is open. A `Cite` with no source gets a dashed '?' marker and says it has nothing behind it, so unsourced statements can't pass for cited ones. Use it in AI answers, research summaries and reports. For 'why this?' about a whole answer, use AI Context Surface instead.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Pass the exact retrieved passage as `quote` — that is what makes checking take one step. Set `support="paraphrased"` when the claim is the model's summary. Leave `source` off rather than attaching a loosely related source.

meta.engineeringNotes: Designed from one research finding: people rarely verify citations, so a numbered marker is mostly a comfort signal that makes answers look more trustworthy than they are. The design makes the check cheap enough to actually happen. The supporting passage itself appears in the popover beside the claim, so comparing the two needs no navigation. The link opens the source at that passage using a URL text fragment, with start and end words for long quotes because fragments must match exactly. Support is a tier, not a score: 'quoted' vs 'paraphrased'. A claim without a source is marked with a dashed '?' rather than left bare, because an uncited sentence sitting among cited ones borrows their credibility. Numbering comes from the order of the `sources` array rather than render-order registration, so it is identical on server and client. The popover stays in the DOM next to its marker, so Tab moves from marker into the link. It is displayed with the Popover API's top layer and fixed coordinates, which keeps it clear of overflow-hidden containers and transformed ancestors. Without Popover API support it falls back to fixed positioning. It opens on mouse hover after a short delay, with a grace period so the pointer can move into it, and on keyboard focus-visible or tap. Clicking outside dismisses it, and Escape closes it and returns focus. The always-visible reference list is the fallback where hover doesn't exist and the audit view where it does.
meta.motionNotes: Minimal, because reading is the user's turn. The popover fades in at `--pd-duration-fast` on the decelerate curve, with no scale or slide, so the quote is readable from its first frame. Hover opens after 180ms, so markers don't flash as the pointer crosses text, and closing waits 140ms so the pointer can travel into the popover. The claim highlight and the marker's active fill change colour at `--pd-duration-instant`. Nothing shimmers: citations describe finished content. All motion becomes instant under prefers-reduced-motion.

items.name: intent-preview
items.title: Intent Preview
items.description: An agent restates what it understood — and the guesses it made — before any work starts. Takes an `interpretation` (the request restated as one plain sentence), optional `assumptions` (each a labelled best guess, optionally with alternative readings the user can switch to in place), optional `boundaries` listing what the agent will deliberately not do, and `onStart`, which receives the confirmed values, plus optional `onRephrase` and `onCancel`. The guesses arrive pre-filled, so when they are right confirming costs one click; when one is wrong it is corrected with a native select rather than by rewriting the prompt, and the start button changes to 'Start with changes' so the difference is visible. The reason it exists: a model that misreads a request early builds every later step on that mistake, so the cheapest correction in an agentic run is the first one. Distinct from Agent Ask, which blocks until the user supplies something the agent cannot guess — this is for when the agent could proceed on its best guess, but being wrong would be expensive. Holds perfectly still, since it is the user's turn. Composes AI Action Toolbar. Use it before long runs, runs with side effects, or requests with ambiguous scope. Not for every request — adding a confirmation to a cheap, reversible action is friction that trains people to click through without reading.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Use it only where misreading the request would be costly — long runs, side effects, ambiguous scope. On cheap, reversible actions it is friction.

meta.engineeringNotes: Built from the model-side view of how agentic runs fail: interpretation happens before planning, and an early misreading compounds through every step that follows. Surfacing the interpretation in one sentence, together with the specific guesses that filled gaps in the request, moves correction to the single point where it is nearly free. Two decisions keep that from becoming friction. First, assumptions arrive pre-filled with the agent's best guess, so the common case — the guess is right — costs one click, and the start label changes to 'Start with changes' only when something was corrected, so the confirmation carries information rather than ceremony. Second, correction happens in place through a native select of alternative readings rather than by rephrasing the whole request, which is both faster and more precise. Boundaries ('I won't…') are included because what an agent will not do is part of its intent and is the thing users most want to know before a run with side effects. It is deliberately distinct from Agent Ask: Ask blocks on missing information the agent cannot guess, whereas Intent Preview is for requests the agent could act on immediately, where acting on a wrong guess would be expensive.
meta.motionNotes: Still, by design. This is a user-turn surface under the system's turn-taking grammar, so nothing moves or shimmers while it waits — the absence of motion is the signal that nothing proceeds until the user confirms. The only motion is the shared colour transition on hover and focus at `--pd-duration-instant`, inherited from the composed AI Action Toolbar and the select's own focus ring, and it drops to instant under prefers-reduced-motion. Entrance motion belongs to whatever surface reveals the preview, not to the component.

items.name: live-status-line
items.title: Live Status Line
items.description: A single line saying what an agent is doing right now — the status bar of an agent run. Takes a `state` from Agent Presence's vocabulary, a `status` describing the current micro-action, an optional `detail` naming what the action is acting on (a filename, a query, a table), an optional `startedAt` that drives a live elapsed counter, and an `onCancel` shown whenever the agent is active. It replaces rather than accumulates, which is the whole distinction from its neighbours: Reasoning Stream keeps a scrollable trace, Chain-of-Thought Timeline keeps the entire turn's history, and this keeps exactly one thing — which is what makes it cheap enough to leave in permanent product chrome like a toolbar, sidebar footer, or table row. Composes Agent Presence in its `line` form for the indicator rather than reimplementing one, so the turn-taking grammar (motion means the machine is busy, stillness means it's your turn) holds here automatically. The status text is keyed so React's reconciliation runs its swap animation exactly once per real change; a re-render with unchanged text never re-animates. Layout is deliberately stable: the row holds a minimum height so changing text length cannot reflow its container, and the detail truncates before the verb does so 'Reading' stays legible even when the filename cannot. Unlike most components in this system the elapsed counter ticks internally rather than being caller-owned, because forcing a re-render once a second for a display detail would be a poor API. Use it wherever an agent's current activity should be visible without dedicating a panel to it. Not for the reasoning text itself (use Reasoning Stream), not for a per-artifact generation progress surface (use Generation Placeholder), and not as a general toast or notification.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`, the `pd-status-swap` keyframe from @pixeldosa/pixeldosa-theme, and @pixeldosa/agent-presence, which it composes for the indicator. Installing this pulls Agent Presence in automatically.

meta.engineeringNotes: The defining constraint is that this component replaces rather than accumulates. Accumulation is what makes agent activity surfaces expensive — a growing list needs scroll management, virtualisation at length, and a decision about when to collapse. Holding exactly one line keeps it cheap enough to live permanently in product chrome, and pushes the history question to Reasoning Stream and Chain-of-Thought Timeline where it belongs.
