It composes Agent Presence's `line` form rather than drawing its own dots, which is the system's compose-don't-reinvent rule applied where it genuinely fits: the turn-taking grammar then holds here for free, including the fact that a `suggesting` or `awaitingApproval` status stops moving. Two layout decisions prevent the jitter this pattern usually has: a minimum row height, so text of varying length cannot reflow the container around it, and truncation applied to the detail rather than the verb, so 'Reading' remains legible when a long filename cannot be. The elapsed counter is the one place this system deliberately breaks its own 'the caller owns async state' convention — every other component takes progress, busy and duration as props — because a live counter would otherwise force the consumer to re-render once a second purely for a display detail. The interval is only started while the agent is actually active, and never when no `startedAt` was supplied.
meta.motionNotes: One animation, and it maps to one state change: when the status text is replaced, the new text fades up three pixels over `--pd-duration-fast` with `--pd-ease-decelerate`. Short deliberately — micro-actions can change every second or two, and anything longer would read as churn rather than as replacement. It is keyed on the status string so React's reconciliation fires it exactly once per genuine change; an unchanged status that re-renders does not re-animate, which is the same mechanism Progressive Reveal and Reasoning Stream use. The indicator's own motion is inherited from Agent Presence and is not duplicated here. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the swap is dropped entirely: text simply changes, which loses nothing, because the information was always the words rather than the transition between them.

items.name: overlay
items.title: Overlay Motion Primitive
items.description: The shared enter/exit animation layer for every overlay surface in the system — Dialog, Sheet, Popover and Drawer. Exports OverlayScrim (the backdrop) and OverlayContent (the panel, with a placement prop of center, top, bottom, left or right that controls which axis it translates from) plus a re-exported AnimatePresence. Not a standalone component: it has no dismiss behaviour, focus trapping or portal logic of its own. Compose it underneath a Radix primitive (Dialog.Overlay/Content, Sheet, Popover) so that primitive owns interaction semantics while this owns motion.
items.docs: Render OverlayScrim and OverlayContent inside AnimatePresence, controlled by the same boolean/state that drives your Radix primitive's open prop. Neither component owns mount/unmount timing — AnimatePresence does, via whatever is conditionally rendering them.

meta.engineeringNotes: Extracted as its own primitive rather than duplicated inside Dialog, Sheet, Popover and Drawer because those four are the same motion problem (scrim fade + panel translate/scale) wearing four different Radix primitives underneath. Without this, four components would each hand-roll slightly different durations the first time someone patches one of them, and the system's visual coherence — the actual point of a token-driven motion scale — degrades one component at a time. Deliberately excludes dismiss-on-click-outside, focus trapping and portalling: those are interaction semantics Radix already solves correctly, and re-solving them here would create two competing sources of truth for overlay behaviour.
meta.motionNotes: Two states only: scrim opacity, and content opacity+scale+translate along one axis determined by `placement`. Enter uses duration.fast with easing.decelerate (content is arriving, should feel like it's settling in); exit uses duration.instant with easing.accelerate (dismissal should feel immediate, not lingering) — this asymmetry is deliberate, not an oversight. The motion solves orientation: a Sheet sliding in from the right tells the user where it came from and, on exit, where it's returning to, which a plain fade does not. Reduced motion swaps the whole transition object for the shared `reducedMotion` token (near-zero duration) rather than removing the animation, so Motion's exit callback still fires and AnimatePresence still unmounts the content correctly.

items.name: pixeldosa-agent-guide
items.title: PixelDosa Agent Guide
items.description: An instruction file for AI coding agents building with PixelDosa, installed into a team's repository so their agent knows not just which component to use but how to use it well. Covers registry setup, a job-to-component selection table, when to start from a Block instead of assembling parts, the non-negotiable UX rules (nothing commits silently, never add Accept all, approvals phrased as consequences with reversibility and impact stated, nothing waiting on the user is animated, shimmer only on active status verbs, a visible Stop during every working state, no faked typing, confidence as tiers not percentages), a mapping table from common agent events to component states, and a pre-finish checklist. Installs as a Claude Code skill; other agents can be pointed at the same file or at the site's llms.txt. Contains no code and adds no dependencies.
items.docs: Installs to .claude/skills/pixeldosa/SKILL.md, where Claude Code discovers it automatically. For Cursor, Copilot, or other agents, reference this file from your rules or AGENTS.md, or point the agent at https://pixeldosa.akshayjayan.com/llms.txt.

meta.engineeringNotes: Coding agents already find and install PixelDosa through the shadcn MCP server and CLI search, because every registry description was written for cold LLM comprehension. What they could not do was use the components well: nothing stopped an agent from wiring an AI value straight into data or adding an Accept all button, since those decisions live in the design system's judgment rather than its props. This item transfers that judgment into the consumer's repository as a plain markdown skill, so the rules travel with the code instead of staying on a docs site the agent may never read. It is the same source the site's llms.txt draws its rules from, so the two cannot drift. It ships as registry:file with no dependencies, consistent with the principle that PixelDosa never requires an agent stack.
meta.motionNotes: No motion — this item is a documentation file, not a component. It does, however, carry the system's motion rules to agents in written form: motion means the machine is busy and stillness means it is the user's turn, shimmer is reserved for active status verbs, completed text is never revealed character by character, and prefers-reduced-motion is always respected rather than overridden.

items.name: pixeldosa-theme
items.title: PixelDosa Theme
items.description: The PixelDosa design and motion token layer, installed as CSS custom properties. Provides the full semantic colour scale for light and dark mode (background, foreground, card, popover, primary, secondary, muted, accent, destructive, border, input, ring), the base corner radius, and the duration/easing/stagger variables that every PixelDosa component animates against. Install this once per project before or alongside any other PixelDosa component; installing a component without it leaves the component styled against the host project's existing theme values instead.

.pd-shimmer.background-image: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--muted-foreground) 0%, var(--muted-foreground) 35%, var(--foreground) 50%, var(--muted-foreground) 65%, var(--muted-foreground) 100%)

items.docs: The cssVars in this item are generated from packages/tokens. Do not edit them here — change the token module and rebuild.

meta.engineeringNotes: Shipped as a registry:theme item rather than baked into each component so that colour is a project-level decision made once, not a per-component import that would break the moment a consumer wants their own palette. Colours are OKLCH rather than HSL so the light and dark scales can be derived from matched perceptual lightness steps; the practical payoff is that a token pair like muted/muted-foreground holds its contrast ratio across both modes without per-mode hand-tuning. Motion values are emitted as CSS custom properties in addition to the TypeScript exports, so components that need only a CSS transition can honour the motion scale without pulling in a JS animation runtime.
meta.motionNotes: This item defines the motion scale rather than animating anything itself. Durations are exposed in milliseconds (CSS) and seconds (TypeScript/Motion) from one source, because emitting only one unit guarantees a conversion bug at the first component that needs the other.

items.name: progressive-reveal
items.title: Progressive Reveal
items.description: Reveals a growing collection of items (rows, cards) one at a time as they arrive from a streaming or incrementally-loading source, with a stable layout and no per-character typewriter effect. Takes items (the current known array, expected to grow over time via the consumer's own state), a renderItem(item, index) function for the actual per-item markup, an optional keyExtractor for stable identity, and an isStreaming flag that shows a trailing 'More loading…' indicator while more items are expected. Each item is given its entrance transition exactly once: React's own keyed reconciliation means an item already present on a prior render keeps its existing DOM node and never remounts, so its animation can never replay. A layout prop switches between a vertical stack (default) and a CSS grid for card collections. Use for streaming search results, tool-call output rows, or generated card grids — any collection whose full membership isn't known upfront. Not for streaming prose (use an existing chat/response component) or a single changing value (that's Smart Field or Diff Accept's job, not a collection).
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Is a plain generic function component (no `forwardRef`) since nothing here needs an imperative handle and `forwardRef` has poor generic-type ergonomics. Pass a real `keyExtractor` whenever the source array might ever be spliced rather than purely appended — without one, index-based keys can misattribute 'already seen' identity to the wrong item if earlier entries are removed or reordered.

meta.engineeringNotes: Enforces 'animate a new item in exactly once' by relying on React's own keyed reconciliation instead of hand-rolled 'already seen' tracking: each item is wrapped in a small RevealItem component keyed by keyExtractor (or index), which mounts fresh — and therefore plays its entrance transition — only the first time its key appears in the list; on every subsequent render where that key was already present, React reuses the existing DOM node and the component is not remounted, so the animation structurally cannot replay. This is simpler and more reliable than maintaining a Set of seen keys by hand, which is easy to get subtly wrong around React's own re-render timing. Scoped deliberately to structured collections (rows, cards), not prose — an append-only list of discrete items is inherently more layout-stable than a single growing text block, since new rows appear below existing content without reflowing it, which is also why this differs from and does not compete with Vercel AI Elements' prose-streaming components (see the roadmap's North Star Reconciliation table).
meta.motionNotes: Per-item entrance is a plain opacity + small upward translate (translate-y-1 to 0) using the same two-phase-mount pattern (mount closed, flip to open on the next animation frame) Command Menu and Selection Actions already use, on --pd-duration-fast/--pd-ease-standard. No item's own content is ever revealed character-by-character — the full item value already exists at arrival time, so a typewriter effect would misrepresent it as being generated live, the same reasoning every other AI-tier component in this system has already established independently. The trailing streaming indicator uses Tailwind's built-in animate-pulse (core Tailwind, no plugin required) gated by motion-safe:, falling back to a static reduced-opacity dot under motion-reduce: — the 'more is coming' text itself is unaffected either way, so the signal survives motion removal.

items.name: prompt-composer
items.title: Prompt Composer
items.description: A request composer that isn't a blank chat box. Free text for what only words can say, structured `controls` for what shouldn't need prompt engineering (tone, length, audience, format), and attachments for context. Each control is a labelled pill ('Tone: Friendly') backed by a native select, and a pill changed from its default is outlined, so the specification can be read at a glance. `onSubmit` receives `{ text, values, attachments }`. The text area grows with its content up to a cap. Enter sends and Shift+Enter adds a line, except during IME composition. Attachments come in through the attach button, drag and drop, or paste. You upload them via `onAttachFiles` and pass `attachments` back with status uploading, ready or failed. Sending is blocked while an upload runs, and the composer says why. `suggestions` fill the text but never send, the character count appears only near `maxLength`, and while `busy`, Send becomes Stop. Use it for generation features: drafts, images, reports. Not a chat input: no thread, no history.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Put anything users would otherwise type as boilerplate ("make it friendlier, keep it short") into `controls`, and turn `values` into the prompt on your side. Upload in `onAttachFiles` and keep `attachments` in your state.

meta.engineeringNotes: Exists because the system argues against making every AI feature a blank chat box and needed an alternative. The composer splits a request into what only words can say (the text) and what is really a specification (controls), because specifications typed as prose are inconsistent and invisible until the result comes back wrong. Controls are native selects inside labelled pills, so they are keyboard, screen reader and phone friendly with no custom listbox. A changed value gets a stronger outline, so the non-default parts of the request stand out. Details are handled where composers usually slip. Enter is ignored while `isComposing`, so IME users confirming a candidate don't send half a sentence. The text area autosizes from scrollHeight up to 240px, because `field-sizing: content` isn't universal yet. Send is `aria-disabled`, not `disabled`, so it stays focusable and the blocked reason ('Waiting for attachments to finish uploading') is shown and announced. The count appears only in the last 10% before `maxLength`. The file input is reset after each pick, so the same file can be picked again. Uploads are the caller's, and the composer only reflects their status. It stays headless about what happens next: the caller assembles the prompt from `values`.
meta.motionNotes: Quiet, because composing is the user's turn. The only moving element is the shared `pd-shimmer` on an uploading attachment's 'Uploading' label, which is real machine work. Borders and backgrounds change colour at `--pd-duration-instant` on focus, hover, drag-over and control changes. The text area grows instantly as lines are added, with no height transition, so the caret never lags the text. Send swaps to Stop without animation, so the control is usable the moment generation starts. Everything is instant or static under prefers-reduced-motion.

items.name: reasoning-stream
items.title: Reasoning Stream
items.description: An agent's reasoning shown as it arrives — a two-line ticker while it streams, folding to a single 'Thought for 12s' line once the answer exists, expandable on demand to the full trace. Takes `steps` (reasoning summary lines, oldest first, appended as they arrive), `isStreaming`, an optional measured `durationMs` shown on completion, and `defaultExpanded`. The default is collapsed, deliberately: reasoning is scaffolding that is useful while a thing is being built and noise once it stands, and a reasoning panel left expanded after the answer lands makes every answer look like it needs justifying. Handles scroll anchoring correctly — it follows new content only while the reader is at the bottom, and the moment they scroll up it holds their position and offers a 'Jump to latest' affordance instead of yanking them back. Steps fade in whole and exactly once, enforced by React's keyed reconciliation rather than a timer; text that has already arrived is never revealed character-by-character, since that would misrepresent content the model already finished producing. `steps` is an array rather than a raw string because providers emit reasoning summaries as discrete parts and deciding where one thought ends belongs to the caller. Maps to OpenAI Responses reasoning-summary deltas and the AI SDK's `reasoning` part type, with no AI dependency of its own. Use it wherever a model exposes reasoning and seeing the work builds warranted trust. Not for the agent's activity state (use Agent Presence), not for the full historical record across a whole turn (use Chain-of-Thought Timeline), and not for a collapsed 'why this?' over an already-finished value (use AI Context Surface).
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils` and the `pd-fade-in` keyframe supplied by @pixeldosa/pixeldosa-theme's css block. Show reasoning *summaries* where the provider exposes them; raw private chain-of-thought should not be presented to end users as fact.

meta.engineeringNotes: The component's thesis is the fold-away on completion, not the ticker. Reasoning text is long, low-value-per-token, and usually not what the user wants to read, which creates a bind: showing all of it buries the answer, showing none of it is the black box that destroys trust. Collapsing to a measured 'Thought for 12s' resolves both — the duration answers 'was this worth waiting for' better than any amount of reasoning text, and the disclosure keeps the trace available for anyone who actually wants it. Scroll anchoring is implemented as a correctness requirement rather than a nicety: the component tracks distance-from-end on scroll and only follows new content while the reader is within 24px of the bottom, because auto-scrolling someone who has deliberately scrolled up to read something is the most hostile thing a streaming surface can do. That behaviour came from a competitive scan of a peer library's Message Scroller and now applies as a standing requirement to every streaming surface in this system, not as a component of its own. Each step is its own keyed child component so React's reconciliation owns the entrance animation — a step already on screen keeps its DOM node and can never replay its fade however often the parent re-renders, which is the same mechanism Progressive Reveal uses and which a timer-based approach gets wrong on the first re-render. `steps` is an array rather than a raw accumulating string so the component never has to guess where one thought ends.
meta.motionNotes: Steps fade in whole over `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-decelerate`, exactly once each. They are never typed out character-by-character: the text has already been produced by the time it reaches this component, and animating it as though it were being composed live would misrepresent what actually happened — the same non-negotiable rule Ghost Input, Smart Field, Diff Accept and Progressive Reveal all hold. The expand/collapse uses the house `grid-template-rows` 0fr→1fr transition at `--pd-duration-fast`, so no height measurement or ResizeObserver is needed and the panel animates correctly at any content length. The ticker's top edge is a CSS mask rather than an animated fade, so older lines dissolve out without anything moving. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the step fades and the expand transition are both dropped; steps appear instantly and the disclosure snaps, and since the information was never carried by the motion, nothing is lost.

items.name: selection-actions
items.title: Selection Actions
items.description: A floating, selection-triggered toolbar for AI actions on a piece of text: select text inside a given container and a toolbar of consumer-defined actions (e.g. Explain, Rewrite, Translate, Classify, Extract) appears anchored to the selection. Takes a containerRef (scopes selection detection to one region of the page), an actions array ({id, label, icon}), and an onAction(actionId, selectedText, signal) handler returning a SelectionActionResult shaped as one of: { kind: 'replacement', value } which renders through Diff Accept for accept/reject review, { kind: 'text', value } shown as prose, { kind: 'classification', label, confidence? } shown as a label with a tiered confidence indicator, or { kind: 'list', items } shown as a bullet list. An optional onReplace(mergedValue, originalSelectedText) callback fires only when an accepted replacement is applied, letting a plain-string content model splice the result back in. Use for read or editable content surfaces where per-selection AI actions add value without a context switch to chat. Not for a whole-field or whole-document action (use smart-field or diff-accept directly for that).
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils` and the `diff-accept` primitive at `@/components/ui/diff-accept` (installed automatically as a registry dependency), used to render the 'replacement' result kind. Renders via a React portal to document.body with `position: fixed`, so it is not clipped by an `overflow: hidden` ancestor. Keyboard-only users generally cannot create an arbitrary text selection in static, non-editable content — a platform-level limitation this component cannot fix; the guarantee it makes is that once any selection exists, the toolbar itself is fully keyboard-operable.

meta.engineeringNotes: Composes Diff Accept for the 'replacement' result kind (Rewrite) rather than reimplementing accept/reject a second time — Rewrite is exactly the 'AI proposes replacement text, human reviews' problem Diff Accept already solves, and the two components sharing one review UI keeps the whole AI tier consistent instead of each component inventing its own version of the same interaction. Selection detection listens to document-level `selectionchange`, filtered to whether the selection's anchor node falls inside `containerRef`, debounced (default 200ms) so the toolbar appears once the selection has settled rather than jittering while the user is still dragging or extending with the keyboard — one mechanism covers both input methods, since `selectionchange` fires for either. The toolbar's root uses `onMouseDown` with `preventDefault` — the standard rich-text-editor-toolbar trick — because without it, focusing a toolbar button would collapse the browser's live selection before the click handler ever runs, since focusing an element outside the current selection normally clears it. `onReplace` deliberately takes the original selected text as a second argument rather than assuming a plain string content model on the component's own side: this component cannot know whether the consumer's content is a plain string, a contentEditable region, or a structured rich-text document, so it hands back enough context (the exact original substring) for a plain-string consumer to splice correctly via `content.replace(original, merged)`, while a richer content model would use its own document API and ignore the second argument.
meta.motionNotes: The toolbar mounts in a closed visual state and flips to open on the next animation frame (a `visible` state lagging one rAF behind the selection existing), the same two-phase-mount pattern `Command Menu` uses, so the fade+scale-in (`--pd-duration-fast`/`--pd-ease-standard`) actually has a 'from' value to animate away from rather than popping in already-visible. No motion plays while the selection itself is still changing — the toolbar simply doesn't exist yet during that phase (enforced by the debounce), which is the correct behaviour research on floating selection toolbars confirms (centre after the selection settles, not during), achieved structurally rather than via a suppressed-animation flag. Result content (prose, a classification label, a list, or the composed Diff Accept panel) swaps in via a plain state change, never a per-character reveal, consistent with every other AI-tier component's 'the value already exists in full' reasoning. Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, the fade/scale transition drops via `motion-reduce:transition-none` (scale pinned via `motion-reduce:scale-100`), leaving the toolbar's appearance instant but still fully legible.

items.name: smart-field
items.title: Smart Field
items.description: An AI-proposed value for a single text field, shown with a confidence tier and its source before it becomes real data. The field's value never changes until the user explicitly accepts the proposal — clicking the trigger icon requests one via a consumer-supplied fetchProposal(currentValue, signal) function, which resolves to a SmartFieldProposal { value, confidence?: 'low' | 'medium' | 'high', provenance?: string } or null/undefined for no proposal. Once shown, the proposal renders in a panel below the field with Accept/Reject controls; accepting commits proposal.value into the field and shows a brief Undo affordance. Typing manually at any point (while loading or once a proposal is shown) cancels the in-flight request or dismisses the unaccepted proposal, since manual input always overrides an AI suggestion. Use for CRM/record enrichment, settings or profile fields, or any single structured field where AI has enough surrounding context to propose a value. Not for inline predictive continuation while typing (use ghost-input instead), multi-field or long-text diffing, or a consequential/risky action needing full review.
items.docs: value/onValueChange are required — this is a controlled component only, matching ghost-input's contract. fetchProposal must resolve to the FULL proposed value (not a delta) plus optional confidence/provenance; return null/undefined for 'no proposal available' rather than throwing. triggerIcon is required with no bundled default — pass any size-4 SVG/icon element. autoPropose only fires once, on mount, and only when value is empty, so it can never silently overwrite existing data. Drops into <FieldControl> directly since id/aria-invalid/aria-describedby/ref all forward to the underlying <input>.

meta.engineeringNotes: Mirrors ghost-input's contract shape (value/onValueChange controlled-only, a fetchX behaviour injected by the consumer, an AbortSignal for cancellation) deliberately, so the AI tier reads as one consistent family rather than each component inventing its own pattern — the two differ only in what they return: a plain continuation string for ghost-input versus a structured { value, confidence, provenance } proposal here, because a complete replacement value needs that context attached and a continuation tail does not. Confidence rendering composes the shared `confidence-meter` primitive (extracted after Selection Actions needed the identical tiered indicator) rather than hand-rolling its own bars a second time — a three-tier enum (low/medium/high), not a raw number, because a fabricated percentage would claim precision the underlying model doesn't actually have, and because the system has no colour scale to spend on a red/yellow/green treatment anyway. autoPropose is opt-in and gated to empty fields only, adopted directly from CRM-enrichment research (Clay/HubSpot/Attio): confidence gates whether a proposal is allowed to overwrite existing data, so the safest default auto-behaviour is 'only ever fill a blank,' never 'silently reconsider what's already there.' Manual typing at any point cancels an in-flight fetch or dismisses a shown-but-unaccepted proposal, reusing ghost-input's staleness philosophy: a suggestion answering a question the field no longer asks is worse than no suggestion. The proposal panel animates open/closed via a CSS grid-template-rows trick (0fr to 1fr) rather than measuring and animating an explicit pixel height, which is the standard token-free way to animate a height that depends on variable content without a ResizeObserver.
meta.motionNotes: The proposal panel's height expansion and the field's colour tint both use --pd-duration-fast/--pd-ease-standard; the trigger's busy spinner and accept/reject colour changes use --pd-duration-instant, matching Button's press-feedback timing, because those are immediate state confirmations rather than content arriving. The proposed value itself never animates in character-by-character — the full value already exists the moment it's returned, so a typewriter reveal would misrepresent it as being generated live, the same reasoning ghost-input's plan already established. Confidence Meter (composed, not reimplemented here) has no motion of its own — under prefers-reduced-motion, the panel's grid-template-rows transition and the colour transitions are dropped via motion-reduce:transition-none, leaving the underlying state (panel present/absent, tint present/absent) fully legible without animation.

items.name: thinking-experience
items.title: Thinking Experience
items.description: A complete agent run, orchestrated — the first Level 2 Block in this system, and the composed surface the AI-tier components exist to be assembled into. Takes one `state` from the agent vocabulary plus a `status` line, optional `reasoning` steps, an optional `ask` request, an optional `approval` request, and a terminal `result` with its action strip, then decides which of those surfaces belongs on screen at each moment. The value over rendering the same components yourself is entirely the orchestration: a consumer wiring Live Status Line, Reasoning Stream, Agent Ask and AI Approval Gate together has to re-derive when each appears, when reasoning should stop streaming, when the elapsed counter should freeze, and what happens to the machine's own surfaces while a human is being asked something — and that last question is the one most implementations get wrong. This block applies the turn-taking grammar at the level of the whole panel rather than a single indicator: when control passes back to the user, the machine's status and reasoning visibly step down in emphasis and whatever needs an answer takes a ring, while remaining fully interactive so a run can always be stopped even while it waits on you. Composes Live Status Line, Reasoning Stream, Agent Ask, AI Approval Gate and AI Action Toolbar, which transitively pulls in Agent Presence, Confidence Meter and AI Context Surface. Use it as the agent panel in a product — a sidebar, a drawer, an inline run surface. Not a chat thread and not a transcript: it shows one run in progress, not a history of turns.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Installing this pulls in the whole AI-tier stack it composes — Live Status Line, Reasoning Stream, Agent Ask, AI Approval Gate and AI Action Toolbar, plus Agent Presence, Confidence Meter and AI Context Surface transitively. Drive it from a single agent state; passing `ask` and `approval` alongside is harmless, since only the one matching the current state renders.

meta.engineeringNotes: The first Block in this system, and it is deliberately an orchestration rather than new UI: every visible element comes from an already-shipped component. What it contributes is the set of decisions a consumer would otherwise have to re-derive — which surface belongs on screen at which state, that reasoning stops streaming the moment control passes to a human rather than continuing to tick behind a question, that the elapsed counter freezes on terminal states instead of counting forever, and that a pending question or approval is what the eye should land on. The interesting decision is how the turn-taking grammar scales: at component level it is one indicator moving or holding still, but at panel level it becomes relative emphasis, so the machine's status and reasoning drop to 55% opacity while an interrupt takes a ring. They are dimmed but deliberately never disabled — a run must remain stoppable even while it is waiting on the person, and `pointer-events-none` on that region would have silently removed the Stop control at exactly the moment someone might want it. Emphasis is carried by a ring rather than by animation because this is the user's turn and stillness is the signal; animating the thing that wants attention would contradict the grammar the rest of the system holds. Ask and approval are passed as plain data objects rather than as slots so the block owns the decision of when each appears — a slot-based API would hand the orchestration question straight back to the consumer, which is the one thing this component exists to answer.
meta.motionNotes: Two transitions, both mapped to a real state change. The machine region cross-fades its opacity over `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-standard` as control passes between the agent and the user, which is the panel-level expression of the turn-taking grammar and the only motion that belongs to this block itself. The result fades in once over `--pd-duration-base` with `--pd-ease-decelerate` when the run reaches a terminal state. Everything else is inherited: Live Status Line's status swap, Agent Presence's rotation, Reasoning Stream's step fades and disclosure, AI Action Toolbar's colour transitions and busy spinner. Nothing is duplicated at this level, which is the point of composing rather than reimplementing — one rhythm, set once in the tokens, applied consistently by every part. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the block's own two transitions drop to instant and each child handles its own fallback, leaving the layout, the ring emphasis and the opacity difference fully legible without any movement.

items.name: tool-call-card
items.title: Tool Call Card
items.description: What an agent actually did — read a file, ran a search, fetched a page, wrote a change — shown as a record beside what it says. `ToolCallCard` takes a `kind` (read, search, fetch, write, run, call), the exact `target` it touched, a `status` (running, done, failed, blocked), and optional `name`, `input`, `output`, `error` and `durationMs`. It leads with a plain sentence, verb then target, and keeps the arguments and result one click away. `effect` defaults from the kind: read-only calls stay quiet, while calls that made changes or reached outside the app carry a label, because those are what a reviewer hunts for. `ToolCallGroup` folds a run's calls into one line ('Read 2 files, searched once, wrote 1 file') with counts of calls that made changes and calls that failed, and shows the running call in place of the tally. Use it next to agent answers so retrieved knowledge is distinguishable from asserted knowledge. Not a log viewer or a debugging console.
items.docs: Requires `cn` at `@/lib/utils`. Map each tool your agent exposes to a `kind`, and override `effect` for tools whose side effects the kind doesn't imply (e.g. a `run` that is read-only). Show the group next to the answer it supports, not in a separate debug panel.

meta.engineeringNotes: Built for a trust gap seen from the model side. An agent's answer blends what it retrieved with what it inferred, and the text alone reads the same either way. A visible record of the calls lets a reader tell 'the config sets a 30s timeout' backed by a read of config.ts from the same sentence with nothing behind it, and it makes failures just as visible: the demo's answer admits the docs fetch failed, and the failed card is right there. Three decisions keep this from becoming a log dump. The summary is a sentence, verb then exact target in monospace, so it scans like prose. Evidence (arguments and result) sits in a disclosure, capped in height with its own scroll so one large result cannot swamp the run. And effect is a first-class prop defaulted from the kind, so the handful of calls that changed something are labelled among the many that only looked. Blocked calls never ran, so they never carry an effect label. The group tallies only finished calls and reports failures separately, so the headline never counts a failed read as a read. Collapsible regions use the house 0fr→1fr grid with overflow-hidden, padding inside the min-h-0 child, and inert while closed.
meta.motionNotes: Motion only where the machine is working. A running call's verb takes the shared `pd-shimmer`. The target never shimmers, because it is content and must stay readable. While any call runs, the group headline swaps its tally for that call, so the one moving line is always the current action. Disclosures open with a grid-template-rows transition at `--pd-duration-fast` and a chevron rotation on the same curve. Hover colour runs at `--pd-duration-instant`. Finished, failed and blocked calls hold still. Everything falls back to instant or static text under prefers-reduced-motion.
